title: Jacob & Youngs, Inc. v. Kent
summary: An innocent substitution of equivalent pipe could be substantial performance; the owner’s monetary allowance depended on the significance of the defect and the disproportionate cost of replacement.
notes: The editors reproduce additional contract specifications at p. 853, including prior written approval for substitutions, architect decision clauses, and replacement language. Those provisions sharpen the question whether the majority’s interpretation respected the bargain. The notes also explain that Restatement § 241 treats good faith as a factor rather than making every deliberate deviation categorically fatal.

sections.Parties: Jacob & Youngs built Kent’s country residence and sought the unpaid construction balance. Kent was the owner who demanded replacement of plumbing that did not bear the specified manufacturer’s name.
sections.Material Facts:
The residence cost more than $77,000, with $3,483.46 unpaid. Construction ended in June 1914 and Kent occupied the house. No complaint about the pipe arose until March 1915. The specifications called for standard wrought-iron pipe of Reading manufacture, but some installed pipe came from other factories. The architect had inspected incoming pipe without detecting the discrepancy; manufacturers’ names were stamped at intervals of several feet.

The architect demanded replacement. Most pipe was enclosed in walls, so compliance would require expensive demolition of completed portions of the house. The builder offered to prove that the installed pipe equaled Reading pipe in quality, appearance, market value, and cost. The majority treated the evidence as supporting an innocent subcontractor oversight. Kent demanded replacement of the entire system rather than limiting his demand to exposed sections that might be changed more cheaply.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court excluded the evidence of equivalence and directed a verdict for Kent. The Appellate Division ordered a new trial. The Court of Appeals affirmed that order and directed judgment absolute for the builder on the stipulation associated with the appeal.
sections.Issue: Did the departure from the specified brand necessarily prevent recovery of the contract balance, and should the allowance for the defect equal reconstruction cost or diminished value?
sections.Holding: The excluded evidence could establish substantial performance. In these circumstances the appropriate allowance was the difference in value rather than replacement expense grossly disproportionate to the benefit.
sections.Reasoning:
Cardozo distinguished a duty to perform completely from a condition requiring literal perfection before any payment is available. A trivial, innocent departure may remain a breach that requires compensation without causing forfeiture of the builder’s entire recovery. Its significance depends on the purpose to be served, the desire the specification protects, the excuse for departure, and the cost of strict adherence.

A completed house cannot be returned in the way defective movable goods often can. Destruction of useful work therefore matters when deciding what performance the law implies as a condition of payment. The court gave no general license to substitute materials considered equally good: a departure that substantially frustrates the transaction, or a clearly imposed express condition, presents a different question.

Completion cost is ordinarily available, but where it is grossly and unfairly disproportionate to the good attained, the measure becomes diminished value. The proffered equivalence evidence could make that difference nominal or zero. That discussion must be read with the posture: the trial court had excluded the threshold proof, so the case was not an ordinary final calculation following a complete damages trial.

textbookImport.basis: Study paraphrase of the supplied tenth-edition casebook. No current-law/citator review.

learning.why: The case links substantial performance, implied conditions, forfeiture, and the choice between cost-of-correction and value-based damages. It explains why a breach and a continuing duty to pay can coexist.

topics.conditions: The court distinguishes a breached specification from a strict condition of all payment.
topics.substantial-performance: An insignificant and innocent defect can leave the owner obliged to pay, subject to compensation.
topics.damages-cost-value: Destructive replacement cost may be displaced by diminished value when the cost is grossly disproportionate.
topics.interpretation: The transaction’s purpose and the specificity of the condition matter.
topics.good-faith: The majority and dissent disagree about the culpability and significance of the substitution.
topics.forfeiture: Withholding the balance for a minor, built-in defect can impose a disproportionate loss.

learning.separateOpinions: McLaughlin’s dissent emphasized that only about 1,000 of 2,000–2,500 feet of pipe complied, regarded the conduct as intentional or equivalent gross neglect, and insisted on the owner’s entitlement to the specified brand. Two other judges joined the dissent.
